title: Physical Adjoint Learning in Wave Systems with Asymmetric Couplings
authors: Lucas J. Fernández-Alcázar, John Guillamon, Krishna Joshi, Tsampikos Kottos
abstract: Developing self-optimizing physical systems that learn directly from their response to external stimuli offers a promising route toward adaptive and intelligent machines. A key ingredient is the ability to evaluate optimization gradients within the physical hardware, bypassing the need for accurate numerical models. In wave systems, \textit{in-situ} adjoint methods provide this capability by exploiting reciprocity to physically realize the adjoint dynamics. However, this approach generally breaks down in nonreciprocal systems, where the adjoint field cannot be directly accessed through the original device. Here, we develop an \textit{in-situ} adjoint optimization framework that extends physical gradient computation to wave systems with asymmetric couplings through computationally low-cost similarity transformations between the forward and transposed operators. We utilize available degrees of freedom like tailored injected excitations, targeted measurements, and tunable parameters, to enable adjoint field reconstruction through forward experiments on the same physical platform. We demonstrate the versatility of the protocol through broadband transmission and isolation, coherent perfect absorption, programmable wavefront shaping, and spatially selective sensing. Our results provide a route to self-optimization in complex nonreciprocal wave systems through efficient physical gradient-based learning. The number of experiments required by the protocol does not increase with the number of optimization parameters, and the method remains applicable even when parts of the system are completely inaccessible.
summary: This paper introduces a novel in-situ adjoint optimization framework for wave systems with asymmetric couplings, overcoming the limitation of standard methods that require system reciprocity. By using similarity transformations and accessible forward measurements, the authors enable physical gradient computation for self-optimization in complex, nonreciprocal hardware. This allows for the design of advanced wave devices, such as those exhibiting programmable wavefront shaping, purely through physical experimentation.
main_problem: Developing self-optimizing physical systems that learn directly from external stimuli, especially in nonreciprocal wave systems where standard adjoint methods fail.
main_result: The authors propose an in-situ adjoint optimization framework that reconstructs the adjoint field using similarity transformations and forward experiments, enabling physical gradient-based learning.
method: The framework extends adjoint methods to nonreciprocal systems by utilizing computationally low-cost similarity transformations between forward and transposed operators to reconstruct the adjoint field.
model_or_system: The study focuses on wave systems, including 1D tight-binding chains and coupled ring resonators, characterized by asymmetric (nonreciprocal) couplings.
key_observables: Transmittances ($T_n$), spectral derivatives (slope and curvature), and the reconstructed adjoint field ($\lambda$).
important_parameters: Asymmetric coupling strengths, onsite potentials ($\omega_n$), and penalty weights ($\alpha,  eta$) for spectral optimization.
main_assumptions: The method relies on establishing experimental accessibility conditions for the similarity transformation, and in some cases, assumes the transformation must hold for all independent parameter tunings.
figures_summary: Figure 2 compares optimized transmission spectra using different objective functions ($g_0, g_1, g_2$), showing that higher-order penalties yield flatter, broader transmission windows.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general need for in-situ adjoint methods in nonreciprocal systems, to applying this framework to optimize broadband transmission in 1D lattices using spectral penalties, and finally analyzing the mathematical constraints on the similarity transformations required for parameter tuning.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, model-free optimization tool for physical wave systems, directly applicable to designing complex photonic or acoustic devices without needing full numerical characterization of the adjoint dynamics.
